title: OpenAI drops 372 math results from an unreleased model, and mathematicians ask for receipts
summary: Scientific American reported October 6 that OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts, grouped into 372 result families, to a GitHub repository at 6 p.m. EDT, each claimed to resolve or make substantial progress on a major open question in mathematics or theoretical computer science. The claims include a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, improvements to important computer algorithms, and progress toward the Riemann hypothesis, and many results are already verified in Lean, a language that checks a proof’s logic. An OpenAI spokesperson said the unreleased model produced almost every result from a single prompt to a single agent, though some may have taken multiple attempts; The Verge reports OpenAI says the average result used the equivalent of three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking. OpenAI did not publish prompts, only average compute, despite an advisory group of mathematicians asking for them. “We should ask for receipts,” said MIT’s Andrew Sutherland, while Toronto’s Daniel Litt called the release “a good thing for mathematics.” Mathematicians will need months to judge which proofs carry genuinely new ideas.

title: Meta, Walmart, Stripe, and Sierra publish an open standard for AI agents that shop for you
summary: Quartz, citing CNBC, reported October 6 that Meta, Walmart, Stripe, and enterprise AI startup Sierra are publishing a “personal agent protocol,” an open standard for how AI agents interact with businesses online. Sierra co-founder and OpenAI chairman Bret Taylor, who leads the effort, said companies have no reliable way to tell whether an AI agent or a human is visiting: “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists.” He compared it to signing into other sites with a Google or Facebook account; the protocol is meant to verify that a bot is acting for a real person and show businesses what agents are doing on their platforms. OpenAI and Anthropic are not on board yet, though Taylor said he expects them to join.

title: S&P 500 and Nasdaq close at records as AI chips and power producers rally
summary: Tuesday’s close put the S&P 500 up 0.58% at a record 7,818.95, its first close above 7,800, with the Nasdaq Composite up 0.45% at a record 27,599.79 and the Dow up 0.49%, per Miracoup’s market wrap; the Russell 2000 fell 0.6%. Utilities led all sectors with a 3% gain after Constellation Energy’s new power deal with Google sent Constellation up about 12%, and AI hardware joined in: Marvell rose 5.8% after its investor day, AMD 2.8%, and Broadcom 3.7%, per Swingfolio. Nvidia edged up 0.14% to a record, with its market value near $6 trillion. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.27%. Third-quarter earnings season starts in earnest in mid-October. GROKI does not print live share prices.

title: Marvell targets up to $90 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031 on AI data-center demand
summary: At its October 6 investor day, Marvell set its first-ever fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion, Quartz reports, far above the $47 billion analyst consensus CNBC cited; Marvell posted $8.2 billion in its most recent fiscal year. It also raised its fiscal 2028 goal to $20 billion from $18 billion, crediting data-center connectivity such as scale-up optics and switching, and kept fiscal 2027 at about $12 billion. Marvell designs custom AI chips for cloud giants including Amazon and Alphabet and makes the optical and networking chips that move data inside data centers. CEO Matt Murphy said its AI market could reach $400 billion by 2030, and the company forecast $3 trillion in data-center capital spending by 2030. These are company targets, not guarantees.

title: Mistral’s Large 4 “Le Chonk” arrives in public preview at 1.05 trillion parameters
summary: Mistral AI announced Mistral Large 4 on October 6, Unite.AI reports, a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model that its documentation lists at 1.05 trillion total parameters with 49 billion active, a 1.6-billion-parameter vision encoder, and a 1-million-token context window. It’s in public preview for all users through Mistral’s API as mistral-large-4, priced at $0.68 per million input tokens and $2.09 per million output tokens, with open weights planned for the end of October. Mistral says it is the best open-weights model from the United States or Europe on aggregated benchmarks, with state-of-the-art results in cyber defense, manufacturing, and finance, and that it was built end-to-end in Europe. Those claims are Mistral’s own, and no checkpoint is on Hugging Face yet.

title: Google’s EmbeddingGemma 2 puts text, code, images, video, and audio in one search space
summary: Google DeepMind launched EmbeddingGemma 2 on October 6, an open 740-million-parameter model that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into one shared embedding space, the kind of index that powers search and retrieval. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it is small enough for on-device use. Google’s examples: finding a specific video clip from a voice memo, or searching hours of audio recordings with a text query, all with a single model. Google says the original text-only EmbeddingGemma has passed 20 million downloads.

title: Reka’s Rho-1 makes video and drives a robot from the same 19B-parameter weights
summary: Reka AI released Rho-1 on October 5 as a research preview, AIvio reports: a 19-billion-parameter model that takes in and produces text, images, video, and robot actions inside one network. The same weights that predict the next video frame also produce the next robot action. To get around scarce robot training data, Reka uses a model that recovers control signals from ordinary internet video. It was trained on 320 Nvidia H100 GPUs over about three months. Reka is candid about limits: structure drifts past about 30 seconds, objects get lost across a video, and native resolution is 672 by 384. No weights are released, and none of the figures has been checked outside Reka.

title: Google funds 890 megawatts of new nuclear power by upgrading 11 existing reactors
summary: Google and Constellation Energy announced on October 6 a 20-year power purchase agreement to add 890 megawatts of new nuclear capacity to the PJM grid by upgrading equipment at 11 Constellation reactors in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey, rather than building a new plant. Constellation says it represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment, about 7,200 construction jobs, and roughly the output of a large new reactor. The first upgrade is expected by 2028, and Google says the full 890 megawatts arrives before the end of 2032. Google also signed a 15-year supply deal for another 2,700 megawatts and will deploy Gemini Enterprise to help Constellation run its plants.

title: Forty-five minutes of learning how to question AI nearly doubled students’ fixes
summary: Scienmag reported October 6 on a randomized trial in the International Journal of STEM Education: 95 university physics students revised test answers after chatting with an AI model, and half first got a 45-minute lesson on prompting it, spotting its reasoning errors and hallucinations, and reflecting on their own thinking. Among trained students, 69.3% of revisions turned a wrong answer right, against 41.3% for the untrained group, and 40% of untrained revisions flipped right answers to wrong by trusting the AI blindly. Trained students asked for insight into a problem twice as often and pushed back when the model misread a figure. The authors caution it was a one-day test at one university. The takeaway for today: treat the chatbot as a partner to question, not an answer machine.

title: DEFCON Acadiana talks AI security in the agentic era tonight at Walk-On’s
summary: DEFCON Acadiana hosts “The Reality of the AI Wave: AI Security in the Agentic Era” on Wednesday, October 7, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. at Walk-On’s Sports Bistreaux, 2336 Kaliste Saloom Road. Felix Simmons, director of emerging technology at GuidePoint Security, with more than 20 years in cybersecurity and contributions tied to the OWASP LLM Top 10, leads an open conversation with audience Q&A on governance, agentic systems, red teaming, and defensive controls. General admission is free, and you don’t need to be an AI expert to attend. It lands the same day the AI desk covers a new open standard for verifying AI agents online.

title: Dry Bones premieres Thursday at the AcA to kick off Festivals Acadiens et Créoles
summary: The Center for Louisiana Studies and Roots of Fire premiere Dry Bones on Thursday, October 8, from 2 to 9 p.m. in the Acadiana Center for the Arts’ Moncus Theater, 101 West Vermilion Street. The new multimedia series has contemporary Louisiana musicians listen to archival recordings from the Center for Louisiana Studies and reimagine them. Afternoon and early-evening sessions screen every episode, with conversations and live performances, before episodes are released one at a time this fall. Featured musicians include Cedric Watson, Steve Riley, Nathan Williams, Lisa LeBlanc, Sabine McCalla, and Feufollet with Julie Aubé. Reservation payments go to the Courtney Granger Memorial Fund.

title: Brooks & Dunn bring the Neon Moon Tour to the Cajundome Thursday
summary: The Cajundome’s calendar lists Brooks & Dunn: Neon Moon Tour on Thursday, October 8, and the ticket listing puts showtime at 7 p.m. with Tucker Wetmore and Caylee Hammack also on the bill. The Cajundome is at 444 Cajundome Blvd., and its box office is at 337-265-2104. The next night, Friday, October 9, the arena hosts WWE Friday Night SmackDown.

title: Chorale Acadienne opens its 48th season Thursday with “Glorious Day!”
summary: Chorale Acadienne opens its 48th season with its fall concert “Glorious Day!” on Thursday, October 8, at 7 p.m. at St. Mary Mother of the Church, 419 Doucet Road. The program celebrates America’s 250th year with spirituals, folk songs, and hymns arranged by Mark Hayes, W. L. Dawson, Hall Johnson, Mack Wilberg, and others. Tickets are $25 general, $20 for seniors 65 and up, and $10 for students, at choraleacadienne.com, 337-349-5342, or at the door.

title: Festivals Acadiens et Créoles brings back Scène ’76 this week
summary: The Advocate reports Festivals Acadiens et Créoles returns to Girard Park October 8–11 under the theme “Revolution and Evolution — Celebrating 250 Years of Cultural Fusion on the Bayou,” one of 34 festivals in the Smithsonian’s Festival of Festivals. New this year: Scène ’76 by the Girard Park pond, honoring the first stage after the festival moved from Blackham Coliseum in 1976; a Folklife Village of Indigenous, Acadian, and Creole crafts; a Language Lounge in the Hilliard’s A. Hays Town Building; and a Waterfowl Heritage Area with duck calls, decoys, and restored pirogues. Scène Atelier talks cover Juré, La-La, the roots of zydeco, and a fiddle summit with Renée Reed.

title: Friday to Sunday at Girard Park: from Les Rôdailleurs to Sonny Landreth
summary: The festival’s own site lists Friday, October 9, with Jourdan Thibodeaux et Les Rôdailleurs and Ruben Moreno’s Zydeco Re-Evolution. Saturday’s long lineup includes Steve Riley and the Mamou Playboys, Geno Delafose & French Rockin’ Boogie, Cedric Watson et Bijou Créole, Chris Ardoin & NuStep Zydeko, and Balfa Toujours. Sunday’s names include Blake Miller & the Old-Fashioned Aces, Sonny Landreth, Michael Doucet, and Jeffery Broussard. Thursday, October 8, opens with the Dry Bones premiere at the Acadiana Center for the Arts, presented by the UL Center for Louisiana Studies.

title: Never-shown Elemore Morgan Jr. photos open at the Hilliard Friday
summary: A new Hilliard Art Museum exhibition of 23 photographs by Louisiana photographer Elemore Morgan Jr. opens October 9 and runs through December 19, The Advocate reports. Many have never been shown publicly and were printed posthumously from his original slides. They capture Cajun and Creole musicians at the Smithsonian’s 1976 Festival of American Folklife on the National Mall. The show was organized with the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, the Center for Louisiana Studies, and the Morgan family.
